overview: This bill aims to lower what people pay for insulin, the medicine many people with diabetes need every day. Starting with plan years in 2028, most private health insurance plans, including employer and individual plans, would have to cover at least one version of each type and form of insulin (such as vials and pens) with no deductible and a patient cost of no more than $35 for a 30-day supply, or 25 percent of the plan's discounted net price if that is lower. Insurers could not require prior approval for these insulins except for safety or reasonable quantity limits. The bill also tries to speed up competition from cheaper drugs by letting the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) brush aside petitions filed mainly to delay generic drug approvals and by fast-tracking review of certain lower-cost copies of biologic drugs (called biosimilars). For people without insurance, it creates a five-year, $100 million grant pilot in 10 states to provide insulin for $35 a month or less, funds a national insulin help hotline and resource center, and orders a government study of uninsured insulin users. As of August 7, 2026, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say no one should have to ration a lifesaving drug because of cost, and that capping copays while speeding up generic and biosimilar competition tackles both what patients pay and the underlying price of insulin.
against: Critics say capping patients' costs can shift the expense onto insurers and, through higher premiums, onto everyone else, and that the bill does not directly require drugmakers to lower their list prices.
